[...] A much more famous case which came before the senate in 16... The protagonist was M. Hortensius Hortalus, grandson of Q. Hortensius, the famous orator of the Ciceronian age. He had already received a grant of the senatorial census from Augustus, to enable him to marry and raise a family and so prevent the extinction of so distinguished a line. Now, when the senate was in session in the Palatine library, where a likeness of the great Hortensius was displayed among those of other famous orators of the past, Hortalus lined up his four children at the door and appealed for more money. It was not of his own will, he said, that he had had a family, but only at the request of Augustus reinforced by his piety towards his ancestors. Had he not obeyed, he would have had enough for his own modest needs and would have been a burden to no one.

The implication of his speech was plain: Augustus had landed him in difficulties, and so Augustus' successor owed him a living. The senate was sympathetic, and its attitude stirred Tiberius to make his position clear. If every pauper in Rome came begging money for his children, the state, he said, would soon be bankrupt. Hortensius' action was not an appeal but a shameless demand that was entirely out of place, since the meeting had been convened to discuss other matters, an attempt to exploit the delicacy of the senate and to force the princeps to draw from the treasury in order not to appear mean. When Augustus had made his gift he had not been under pressure of this sort, and he had not intended that the donation should be repeated whenever Hortalus wished. He himself was not prepared to tolerate a state of affairs in which men did nothing to help themselves and lived in carefree idleness as a burden to the state.

His sternness and the violence of his language shocked the senate - as they clearly did Tacitus too - and after a short pause Tiberius announced that he had made his answer to Hortalus but that, if the senate thought it proper, he would grant his sons 200,000 sesterces each, an offer which Hortalus received in silence.

A little background, My father, brother and sister are all fat, my mother and I are not(I'm a dude).

Growing up, I always believed that the size difference was genetic to some extent. Portion sizes were always similar in our house, even for my father, and a second helping was not uncommon. What I failed to realize at the time was the different lifestyles we led. For example, my siblings didn't play any sports that require breaking a sweat, and my dad was/is a business man who led a relatively inactive life. My mother isn't a big lady, and she doesn't eat much, I played sports. After growing up and living away for a few years, I moved back and discovered a few things that changed my mind.

First was that after getting married, my brother ballooned to double the size he was when I moved away and I am personally unaware of any genetic disorders that can cause 150lbs of weight gain during your mid 20s.

The second was that after moving back, I went and had lunch with my dad one day. We met at a fast food restaurant near his house and, to my surprise, the girl working the register quite clearly recognized my dad. Not in the "I've seen you somewhere before" way, but in the "Here's one of my regulars" way.

This is when it all sort of made sense to me, it's not portion size that is their problem, but the frequency with which they consume those portions as well as the type of food being consumed.

So I no longer believe people are predisposed to being fat. It took me until my 30s but my eyes are now wide open and my sympathy well has run dry.

That's it, been a lurker here for awhile, figured it was about time to share something.

I don't even know how to start this story. When I was 16 years old I started experiencing really nasty panic attacks. They seemed to have a focus on my heart; I would feel my heart skipping beats, fluttering, beating really fast, "spasming" in my chest, and it would send me over the edge. I went to the ER several times in my teens for the issue, and saw cardiologists for it. Some days were worse than others. Sometimes I would go weeks without an "episode". I knew this was happening to me, and I knew it was real, but Drs told me I was fine because a 30 second long EKG didn't show anything. Night after night I would go to sleep wondering if I was going to wake up ever again.

I knew something was wrong. I would get chest pains after too much coffee, or after a hard workout. I knew that wasn't normal. My chest felt tight and tired, but everyone said I was fine.

Things got better in my late teens, but the issue returned in my early 20's and stuck around for a few years. It went away again, but then reappeared in my mid 20's, and it's started to appear again shortly after my 31st birthday. I thought, surely, I am going to be one of those people who goes out for a jog and just drops dead, and I'll be all over the news "Healthy runner drops dead from heart attack at 31". Or worse, I'd be masturbating to Sasha Grey and I'd die in my computer chair, and my mom would find me or something.

Then a routine checkup last month revealed an abnormality in my EKG.

I ended up going back to the cardiologist and being placed on a 24 hour Holter. Miraculously, the day I wore the monitor I was extremely symptomatic. Constant flutters, spasms, starts and stops. Today was my follow up to discuss the findings of my echocardiogram and EKG. I knew this was it. He might tell me "it's just anxiety", but probably I'm walking out of this with a diagnosis.

Well tonight is the first night that I know for sure when I go to bed that I'll wake up in the morning. As it turns out, I do have something abnormal about my heart. I have paroxysmal atrial tachycardia. What this means is that my atria, due to an electrical irregularity, beat very rapidly for a short period of time. I don't actually notice or feel this when it happens. What I feel is my ventricles being driven to a faster beat due to my atrium beating faster. This actually isn't particularly dangerous or bad, but it's important that I avoid nicotine, too much caffeine, and stay fit. The Dr. wants to try me on metroprolol to see if it makes me feel better. It might slow my running down a bit, but at least I'll be comfortable probably for the first time in over a decade.

I feel such a sense of release finally knowing.
The biggest weight of my life was just taken off my shoulders.
